How Mandelson tried to influence Starmer's September 2025 reshuffle
Pippa Crerar
Pippa Crerar is the Guardian’s political editor.
The files release today show Peter Mandelson trying to get involved in Keir Starmer’s reshuffle in September 2025.
In a short exchange of WhatsApps on 5 September 2025, Mandelson told Starmer’s chief of staff at the time, Morgan McSweeney, to “solve your Darren issue” – referring to Darren Jones.
Referring to the then science secretary, Mandelson wrote: “Are you taking peter Kyle away ….?”
In a second message, he said: “You should solve your Darren issue and put him at DSIT (Department for Science, Innovation and Technology).”
Around 45 minutes later, he asked where McSweeney was and added “I am in upstairs meeting room”.
Jones was not made science secretary. Instead he was made chief secretary to the PM.
Kyle was moved in the refshuffle. He became business secretary, and Liz Kendall replaced him as science secretary.
The reshuffle took place was prompted by the resignation of Angela Rayner over her tax affairs. In April this year McSweeney, who at that point had resigned, taking responsibility for the flawed decision to appoint Mandelson as ambassador to the US, told the foreign affairs select committee that Mandelson had not masterminded the reshuffle, though he confirmed he had sent unsolicited suggestions by text.
“He texted me his thoughts,” he told MPs. “I have to say that on reshuffle day I get texted a lot of thoughts from a lot of people”.
McSweeney told the committee that he hadn’t responded to any of Mandelson’s suggestions – which the release appears to confirm – but had been in touch with him at the end of the day. “I think we seized that day quite well,” the messages reveal he told him.
The former No 10 chief also told MPs he “might have” bumped into Mandelson in Downing Street that day, but he could not recall. The newly released messages show that the former ambassador told McSweeney exactly where in the building he was. It is unclear whether the two men actually met.
Tom Brake, chief executive of Unlock Democracy, which campaigns for a more inclusive, participatory democracy, has released this statement about the Mandelson files.
The Mandelson files lay bare the inadequacy of official safeguards against conflicts of interest. While the minister’s commitment to beef up the rules is welcome [see 12.50pm], after repeated promises of reform, we need to see serious action. The lines between public office and private business cannot be allowed to become so blurred that the public is left wondering whose interests are being served.
Burnham says more reform needed to ensure 'vested interests' aren't running Westminster, as new Mandelson files released
Andy Burnham has suggested that the revelations in the Peter Mandelson files have strengthened his conviction that further change is needed to the way Westminster operates.
Speaking to reporters in the Downing Street garden, Burnham said:
I don’t think we have yet seen the change that this system down here needs.
I’ve come back in as something of an outsider into the system and I see a lot of things that I think need to change to improve the political culture of this country, and to strengthen the public interest when it comes to all of these issues.
And I will address those in the 10-year plan for Britain that we bring forward next month.
You know, it will involve political reform, public service reform, because I think there’s a lot further to go until people can have confidence that the Westminster and Whitehall system is run on the way that they think it should be run, and that vested interests aren’t running large within the system, so these are precisely the issues that we will address in next month’s 10-year plan.
Asylum applications down a third, number granted asylum down 40%, and asylum hotel use down 64%, Home Office says
The Home Office has also published its own figures relating to immigration today. Here are some of the notable statistics.
- Around 74,000 people claimed asylum in the UK in the year ending September 2026, around a third lower than in the previous year. But this is still higher than in the 2004 to 2012 period, the Home Office says.
Commenting on these figures, Mihnea Cuibus, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory, said:
The decrease in asylum applications has several possible explanations. It is likely that policy has played at least some role, due for example to a lower grant rate for asylum applications, more restrictive rules on refugees’ ability to reunite with their partners and children, and a more restrictive approach towards universities sponsoring students. However, several other countries have also seen declines in asylum applications and it is likely that some of the change results from fewer people coming into the EU – which can also mean fewer people making the onward journey to the UK.
- Around 35,000 people were granted refugee protection in the year ending September 2026, 40% down on the previous year, the Home Office said. And the grant rate fell to 38%, the lowest level since 2018. In 2022 it was 77%.
- The number of asylum seekers being housed in hotels was around 13,000 at the end of September, down 64% on the previous year, the Home Office said.
According to the Migration Observatory, the number of asylum seekers being housed in hotels from July to September was 18% down on the previous quarter. Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the thinktank, said:
Hotel use is substantially down since Labour came to power but there are two remaining barriers. First, the government continues to face difficulties securing other types of accommodation. HMOs in the community are much less expensive but are difficult to source in a country with a shortage of low-cost housing. Large sites such as former military barracks may expand, although in practice such sites still accommodate only a small share of asylum seekers. Second, the appeals backlog continues to spiral. The government has proposed reforms to the appeals system, but this is a long-term project.
How Foreign Office told Mandelson system to manage his conflicts of interest would be applied in 'light touch way'
Olly Robbins, the Foreign Office permanent secretary, told Peter Mandelson in March last year that the arrangements agreed to manage any conflict of interests caused by Mandelson being ambassador and still owning shares in Global Counsel would be managed in a “light touch way”. At that point Robbins was still hoping that the shares would soon be sold.
Tories accuses Mandelson of 'staggering arrogance', after ex-ambassador publishes article with Brexit advice for PM
In the Commons, Charlie Dewhirst, a shadow minister, replied to Dan Jarvis on behalf of the Conservative party. Here are the main points he made.
- He criticised the fact that Mandelson was allowed to keep his shareholding in Global Counsel. He said:
On 11 March [Darren Jones, the then Cabinet Office minister] told this house that the rules required new civil servants to give up such interests before taking office. Seemingly not this one.
Dewhirst said that in March MPs the foreign secetary was told a sale of the shares had been agreed. That was not right, he said. And he said, when a correction was issued, Mandelson was invited to review it first.
- Dewhirst said he was surprised that only one message sent via Signal has been disclosed.
- He asked Jarvis to give details about what documents the police wanted the government to hold back.
- He accused Mandelson of “staggering arrogance”, referring to an article Mandelson has published on Unherd today advising the PM on EU policy.
And by the way, where is Mr. Mandelson this morning? In print, lecturing the prime minister about how to negotiate with Brussels. No apology, no humility, just more advice. It is staggering arrogance. So will the minister confirm that nobody in this government is taking his advice?
In response, Jarvis said that only a “small number” of documents were still being held back. He said he would not give further details about them.
And he gave Dewhirst a “catagorical assurance” that the government would not be taking advice from Mandelson.
In his article, Mandelson said:
If the government decides that fundamentally changing the UK-EU relationship is desirable and viable, it requires the permission of the British people to do so at the next general election. Prefacing this with informal brainstorming with the EU is a good idea because it will clarify the options available. The public’s definitive verdict would then await a post-negotiation referendum, as Burnham has now clarified.
Throughout, the prime minister in particular, but also the foreign secretary, chancellor and other ministers, will need to demonstrate considerable conviction and persuasiveness about why we need to roll back Brexit. The EU will want to know that the government’s heart really is in a new beginning and that it can secure clear public backing for it.
Jarvis said the government has already tightened procedures relating to ministerial appointments in the light of the way the appointment of Mandelson as an ambassador backfired.
The government has already taken action by strengthening the arrangements governing direct ministerial appointments, including more rigorous due diligence and clearer responsibilities for identifying and managing risks, and in developing a strengthened policy around the management of the conflict of interests.
The FCDO has also confirmed that future diplomatic appointments will not be made or announced before the necessary security clearance has been granted, and is strengthening the arrangements for scrutinising political appointments to senior diplomatic posts, including through a role for the foreign affairs select committee.
Security minister Dan Jarvis says some Mandelson documents still being withheld at request of police
Jarvis said some documents were still being withheld at the request of the police. He said:
A number of further documents remain withheld at the request of the Metropolitan police to avoid prejudicing their ongoing investigation. Those remaining documents will be published once the police confirm that doing so will not risk prejudicing their investigation or any subsequent legal processes.
Jarvis tells MPs the documents out today also include messages sent “through non-corporate channels” (like WhatsApp).
He says this issue is already being reviewed by Sir Anthony Finkelstein, a former government chief scientific adviser for national security. This review will report in January, he says.
Minister tells MPs government's outside interests policy to be beefed up in light of Mandelson Global Counsel issues
In the Commons, Dan Jarvis, the security minister, is making a statement about the latest release of Mandelson documents. He says 32 new documents have been made public. These were previously held back at the request of the police, he says.
He says ministers were not involved in the decisions about which documents would be released in accordance with the humble address.
He goes on:
The documents include correspondence relating to the management of Mandelson’s conflicts of interest, including his ongoing stake in Global Counsel. They underline the importance not only of identifying potential conflicts of interest, but of ensuring that the arrangements put in place to manage them are effective and properly implemented.
He adds:
The Cabinet Office will shortly publish a strengthened declaration and management of outside interests policy, which will apply across government.
How Mandelson decided to 'soften' language on China in speech in response to feedback from ex-Global Counsel colleague
Peter Mandelson consulted a former colleague from his Global Counsel lobbying firm before about the text of his Ditchley Park speech before he delivered it, according to emails released today. In response to the feedback, Mandelson said he would “soften” the language on China.

Peter Mandelson left his north London home within minutes of the publication of the new documents, the Press Association reports. He walked past waiting photographers and did not respond when they said hello.
